summary: Automated steel light on a pier in Saginaw Bay, built 1939-42 under PWA funding; privately owned since a 2015 public sale and 2016 resale; tower closed.

structures.type: steel tower (Pepper: on a concrete pier; LighthouseFriends: on a rock-filled steel caisson capped with concrete)
structures.note: Pepper: pier 50 ft across, tower 61 ft. LighthouseFriends, quoting the 1941 Lake Carriers' Association report: tower 50 ft. The foundation is disputed.

staffing.note: Built as an automated electric station, controlled from Coast Guard Station Tawas.

ownership.note: 2015 public sale defaulted; resold 2016 (NHLPA). LighthouseFriends says privately owned. A 2026 listing says a nonprofit owns it with Skillagalee.

events.note: Congress appropriates $5,000 (18 August 1856) for the Charity Island light, the station this light replaced; not this structure.
Pintsch gas buoy placed at the southeast end of Gravelly Shoal (Pepper). LighthouseFriends describes a gas and bell buoy there in the 1920s.
Built from April 1939 (Pepper). LighthouseFriends dates the work from 1938 to the fall of 1941.
In service October 1939 (Pepper). LighthouseFriends gives commissioning at the opening of navigation in 1942.
Pier walls thickened by seven feet after ice stress; about fifteen years after completion (year approximate, from Pepper).
Declared excess by the Coast Guard in May 2014 and offered for stewardship transfer.
Conveyed by public sale for $16,000; high bidder defaulted before closing.

corrections.why: Pepper reports the light and radiobeacon as active aids to navigation (as of 2001), and the 2026 listing calls it a working light. The record's inactive status conflicts with both and with the 'active aid' wording in the record's own conflicts list.

corrections.proposed: 18.6 (61 ft, Pepper) or 15.2 (50 ft, LighthouseFriends); verify against the Coast Guard Light List
corrections.why: The record's 65 ft (20 m) is neither source's figure; Pepper and LighthouseFriends disagree with each other and with the record.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Pepper gives service from October 1939; LighthouseFriends' own narrative gives work from 1938, completion in the fall of 1941 and commissioning at the opening of navigation in 1942 (its Lake Carriers' Association 1941 quotation describes the station but gives no dates). The story gives both accounts and keeps the record's 1939 pending a primary check.

The NHLPA 2015 table records a private owner for the 2015 sale; the 2015 auction notice said only non-profits could bid; LighthouseFriends says a private owner took the light after the first bidder defaulted; a 2026 listing says a nonprofit owns it. No single source settles the current owner, so the story gives all three accounts and names no individual.
Pepper's 61 ft tower and LighthouseFriends' 50 ft tower (from a 1941 report) disagree; the record's 65 ft matches neither. Flagged in corrections.

notes_for_editor: (1) The named owner: LighthouseFriends names the buyer who took the light in 2016 and says he already owned other Michigan and Delaware lights. The story does not name him: he is a private owner, and the sources do not show that he presents himself publicly as the owner of this light. A human should decide whether to name him. (2) The Michigan Public 2015 notice says only non-profits could bid; the NHLPA 2015 table records a private owner. Unreconciled. (3) The 2026 listing (lighthousedream) is a commercial listing guide; it is the only source for a nonprofit owner and for 'working light' in 2026. Verify with the GSA sale record or the Coast Guard before publishing the owner. (4) Dates: the record's 1939 follows Pepper; LighthouseFriends' 1938 to 1941 and 1942 commissioning come from its own narrative, not from the Lake Carriers' 1941 report it quotes for the station's description (that report was not read directly). (5) Pepper spells the contractor Meagher; LighthouseFriends spells him Meager. (6) Pepper's characteristic (1-second flash every five seconds, 2001) and Wikipedia's red flash every six seconds (leads only; not cited) differ from the record's Fl R 6s; the editor should check the Light List. (7) The 1931 Commissioner quote is second-hand (LighthouseFriends); the 1931 report is not in the local corpus; no Chronicling America hits were found for Gravelly Shoal. (8) Corpus check: the Lighthouse Service Bulletin 1930 to 1939 volumes in the corpus do not name the station. (9) No photos added.
